name: Linux From Scratch
summary: An educational documentation project providing step-by-step instructions for designing, building, and configuring a fully customized Linux operating system entirely from source code.
license: CC-BY-NC-SA-2.0 (book) and upstream open-source licenses (GPL, LGPL, BSD, MIT)

content.introduction: Linux From Scratch (LFS) is an educational documentation and system engineering project that provides step-by-step instructions for building a complete Linux operating system entirely from upstream source code. Initiated in December 1999 by Gerard Beekmans, LFS exposes the low-level mechanics of GNU/Linux by guiding administrators and students through the manual assembly of compiler toolchains, C libraries, system initialization daemons, and core userland utilities.
content.what_is_it: Technically, LFS is not a pre-compiled binary Linux distribution, nor does it publish installable ISO images. The primary deliverable of the project is an instructional book and technical specification (rendered in HTML, PDF, and XML) detailing the exact sequence of compilation commands, patches, and configurations needed to build a running operating system on local storage. The resulting built system is entirely bespoke, consisting of software compiled directly on the target machine without pre-packaged distributor binaries.
content.origin_and_history: Gerard Beekmans founded Linux From Scratch in late 1999 to document how individual software packages interconnect to form a functional Unix-like operating system. The first release, LFS 1.0, was published in December 1999. Over more than two decades, the project evolved into an established educational reference for system programmers, kernel developers, and embedded engineers. Bruce Dubbs, DJ Lucas, Douglas R. Reno, Thomas Trepl, and Pierre Labastie joined as key maintainers, coordinating major toolchain transitions across GCC, Glibc, and kernel generations.
content.governance_and_project_structure: Linux From Scratch operates as an open, community-governed documentation project. Decisions regarding package version increments, build sequence alterations, and errata corrections are deliberated publicly on the `lfs-dev` mailing list. The core team oversees source code repositories, book XML sources, and download mirrors hosted on `linuxfromscratch.org`. The project also coordinates subprojects including Beyond Linux From Scratch (BLFS), Automated Linux From Scratch (ALFS), and Cross Linux From Scratch (CLFS).
content.book_variants_sysvinit_and_systemd:
The project maintains two parallel stable editions of the instructional book:

- LFS SysVinit Edition: utilizes traditional System V init scripts located under `/etc/rc.d`, paired with the `sysvinit` daemon and the `eudev` hardware device manager. It offers a classic Unix initialization model with transparent runlevels.
- LFS systemd Edition: implements modern `systemd` alongside native `udev` for service supervision, journal logging, socket activation, and unit-based dependencies.

Both editions follow an identical toolchain compilation sequence before diverging at the initialization and service configuration chapters.
content.beyond_linux_from_scratch_blfs: A base LFS installation concludes with an operational, bootable command-line system equipped with basic networking and text-mode utilities. To construct a fully featured workstation, development machine, or network server, the community provides Beyond Linux From Scratch (BLFS). BLFS documents the source compilation and dependency chaining of hundreds of additional packages, encompassing graphical servers (Xorg, Wayland), desktop environments (GNOME, KDE Plasma, Xfce), web browsers, programming languages (Python, Rust, Go), and server daemons (Apache, Nginx, OpenSSH, BIND).
content.absence_of_an_official_package_manager: LFS deliberately omits an official package management system. In the core book, software is compiled and installed directly to the target filesystem hierarchy via `make install` or `ninja install`. Package lifecycle management—including dependency resolution, binary inventory, and uninstallation—is left entirely to user discretion. The community documents multiple package management strategies in 'LFS Hints', ranging from manual source trees and symlink farm managers (GNU Stow) to installing third-party binary package engines (such as pacman, rpm, or dpkg) or writing automated shell deployment wrappers.
content.toolchain_bootstrap_and_temporary_tools:
The LFS construction methodology eliminates dependencies on the host operating system through a disciplined, two-stage bootstrap:

1. Stage 1 (Cross-Toolchain): A temporary cross-compilation toolchain—comprising Binutils (Pass 1), GCC (Pass 1), Linux API Headers, Glibc, and Libstdc++—is compiled on the host and installed into an isolated directory (`$LFS/tools`).
2. Stage 2 (Temporary Tools): Using the newly compiled cross-toolchain, essential utilities (Bash, Coreutils, Diffutils, File, Findutils, Gawk, Grep, Gzip, Make, Patch, Sed, Tar, Xz) are built to form an independent temporary environment isolated from host runtime libraries.
content.chroot_isolation_and_final_system_build: Once temporary tools are prepared, the administrator mounts virtual kernel filesystems (`/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/run`) and enters the target environment via the `chroot` (change root) system call. Confinement within `chroot` severs linkages with the host distribution's `/bin`, `/lib`, and `/usr`. Inside this jail, the final, permanent system packages are compiled against the newly installed Glibc and installed into `/usr`. Test suites (`make check` or `make test`) are executed at each step to verify compiler and library integrity.
content.kernel_compilation_and_bootloader_setup: LFS does not provide binary kernel images. The user downloads vanilla Linux kernel source archives from `kernel.org`, accesses the kernel configuration menu (`make menuconfig`), and explicitly enables the device drivers, storage controllers, and filesystem modules required by the host hardware. System startup is managed through the GRUB 2 bootloader, with the user manually writing the configuration file (`/boot/grub/grub.cfg`) for either UEFI ESP or legacy BIOS MBR architectures.
content.determinism_and_reproducibility_nuances: While LFS affords total transparency and granular control over compiler flags (`CFLAGS`, `CXXFLAGS`, `LDFLAGS`), the project does not claim unconditional bit-for-bit binary reproducibility. Without an hermetic build container environment, minor differences in host kernel versions, timestamps recorded in compiled objects, processor microarchitectures, and filesystem directory hashing can lead to minor binary discrepancies across different host environments. However, LFS provides the foundational understanding necessary to build fully deterministic build pipelines.
content.privacy_and_telemetry: The resulting operating system contains zero background telemetry, diagnostic beacons, or automated network tracking. Network access is strictly determined by user-compiled software and explicitly invoked commands. The project's instructional guides neither configure nor endorse usage reporting mechanisms.
advantages: Unrivaled educational transparency: provides an exact understanding of how compiler toolchains, libraries, kernels, and userland binaries interconnect
Total software autonomy: every installed package, compilation flag, and optional feature is determined by the system administrator
Absence of distribution bloat: eliminates unnecessary background daemons, pre-packaged telemetry, and unneeded architecture support
Tailored hardware optimization: allows compiling every package with native processor architecture instruction flags (-march=native)
Choice of initialization: offers dedicated, maintained books for both classic SysVinit and contemporary systemd architectures
Extensive modular growth: Beyond Linux From Scratch provides validated guides for hundreds of enterprise and desktop software packages
disadvantages: Extensive time and resource commitment: compiling the entire operating system from source requires significant CPU hours and active manual effort
No official package manager: updating software and tracking installed files requires self-managed scripts, custom wrappers, or external tools
Manual security patch maintenance: administrators must independently monitor CVE advisories and rebuild vulnerable packages from source
High prerequisite knowledge barrier: requires familiarity with command-line interfaces, Unix shell scripting, partition management, and compilation errors
Lack of commercial vendor support: maintenance and troubleshooting rely entirely on documentation, mailing lists, and community forums
who_is_it_for: Computer science students, instructors, and system administrators seeking a deep architectural understanding of GNU/Linux internals
Embedded systems engineers and distribution developers designing custom Linux appliances or specialized operating systems
Linux enthusiasts desiring complete control over every compiled binary, compiler flag, and system component
Developers needing to study toolchain bootstrapping, Glibc interactions, and cross-compilation mechanisms
who_is_it_not_for: End users seeking a turnkey, rapid installation media to deploy a functional desktop or laptop within minutes
Organizations requiring enterprise vendor service-level agreements (SLAs), automated security errata repositories, and regulatory compliance tooling
Users unfamiliar with command-line build processes, source patching, C compilation errors, and manual kernel configuration

components.name: Vanilla Linux Kernel
components.note: Upstream monolithic Linux kernel configured and compiled directly from kernel.org source archives.

components.name: GNU Toolchain (GCC, Binutils, Glibc)
components.note: Foundational compilation toolchain bootstrapped via a two-stage temporary cross-compilation process.

components.name: Init System (SysVinit or systemd)
components.note: Service manager and process supervisor selected by the user via corresponding book editions.

components.name: GRUB 2 Bootloader
components.note: Unified bootloader configured manually to launch the compiled kernel from UEFI or BIOS partitions.

components.name: BLFS Software Catalog
components.note: Modular documentation catalog extending the base LFS environment into full desktop and server systems.

relations.name: Gentoo
relations.note: Peer source-based operating system utilizing Portage for automated source package management, compared to LFS's manual instructional process.

relations.name: Slackware
relations.note: Traditional Unix-like Linux distribution sharing LFS's philosophy of minimal system abstractions and standard upstream software layouts.

relations.name: Arch Linux
relations.note: Binary minimalist distribution providing user-centric control through the Arch Build System (ABS) and Pacman package manager.

variants.name: LFS SysVinit Edition
variants.description: Standard instructional book utilizing SysVinit, /etc/rc.d init scripts, and eudev device management.

variants.name: LFS systemd Edition
variants.description: Alternative instructional book configuring systemd unit supervision, journal logging, and native udev.

variants.name: Beyond Linux From Scratch (BLFS)
variants.description: Modular extension guide detailing the source compilation of desktop environments, servers, and programming runtimes.

variants.name: Cross Linux From Scratch (CLFS)
variants.description: Specialized subproject documenting toolchain bootstrapping for cross-compiling to alternative CPU architectures.

variants.name: Automated Linux From Scratch (ALFS)
variants.description: Subproject providing the jhalfs automation parser to execute LFS book compilation steps non-interactively.
